title: 263 Forgotten Recipes: NIPS Kolkata Cooks Up a Culinary World Record
excerpt: In a six-hour marathon on September 10, 126 students at Kolkata's NIPS Institute of Hotel Management prepared 263 rare and forgotten Indian recipes — provisionally adjudicated by the World Book of Records London.
body:
• On September 10, NIPS Institute of Hotel Management in Kolkata held a six-hour culinary marathon titled "Rare Cuisines of India — From Kashmir to Kanyakumari."
  • 126 students researched, cooked and displayed 263 rare and forgotten Indian recipes within the six-hour deadline.
  • The attempt was provisionally adjudicated on behalf of the World Book of Records London by Chef Subrata Debnath of IHCL, Executive Chef at Taj City Centre New Town, Kolkata.
  • Students researched each recipe's geographical origin, ingredients, preparation technique and cultural context, creating documentation intended as a study reference.

On September 10, the kitchens at NIPS Institute of Hotel Management in Kolkata turned into a race against the clock. In an intensive six-hour culinary marathon, 126 students prepared, completed and displayed 263 rare and forgotten Indian recipes — an attempt to set a world record for the maximum number of such recipes prepared in a single marathon.

Context & Background

The event, titled "Rare Cuisines of India — From Kashmir to Kanyakumari," deliberately looked past the familiar restaurant staples. The collection drew on recipes connected with regional households, tribal and indigenous communities, rural kitchens, mountain and forest regions and coastal areas — food cultures that are increasingly difficult to find in contemporary urban kitchens and restaurant menus.

The exercise demanded research as much as cooking. Students studied the geographical origins, ingredients, preparation techniques and cultural context of the recipes before cooking them, engaging with the stories behind the food as well as the technique. Several first-year students had joined the institute less than a month earlier, yet worked alongside seniors and faculty through the six-hour deadline. The culinary operation was led by NIPS Food Production faculty — Chef Joseph Uttam Gomes, Chef Afaque Ahmed and Chef Pratip Nath — who guided students through research, authenticity checks, production and presentation.

This is not the institute's first record attempt. In 2012, NIPS students prepared 188 varieties of omelettes in 10 minutes, entering the India Book of Records, and in February 2025 the institute created the largest and most diverse dessert spread, also recognised by the India Book of Records. Founder Director Dr Vivek Pathak called that earlier feat "a testament to the skill, passion, and innovation of our students" — a description that fits the latest effort equally well.

Impact & Analysis

The marathon was provisionally adjudicated on behalf of the World Book of Records London by Chef Subrata Debnath, Area Director – Culinary at IHCL and Executive Chef of Taj City Centre New Town, Kolkata. It was also attended by Prof Shabina Nishat Omar of the West Bengal Education Directorate and veteran hotelier Shekhar Mukherjee, formerly of Taj SATS Kolkata, with guests from the hospitality sector, education and media visiting the displays.

The significance extends beyond the record books. India's culinary identity is built from thousands of regional preparations, many largely undocumented outside the communities that traditionally prepare them. NIPS said the documentation generated through the project is intended to serve as a reference for future students and to support further study of lesser-known regional cuisines. For hospitality professionals, it is also a reminder that culinary education is not limited to modern restaurant technique — understanding traditional ingredients, methods and food histories helps future chefs represent India's culinary diversity with greater depth.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the recipes disappearing fastest are often the ones grandmothers carried in memory and never wrote down — exactly the kind NIPS students researched and documented. Diaspora kitchens in the US, UK and the Gulf already act as quiet archives of regional food; a project like this offers a model for recording those dishes before the last people who know them are gone, and a source diaspora families can draw on to keep their own food heritage alive.

What's Next

The record remains provisionally adjudicated, with final confirmation resting with the World Book of Records London. Whether or not the title lands, the students have already produced something more durable: a documented collection of 263 rare recipes that NIPS plans to use as a teaching reference — a small archive against the steady erosion of India's lesser-known food traditions.
